mainTopic: Signals that complete a sale (key, מַשְׁכּוּכִית), and liability for a covered or uncovered בור
overview: The amud opens with two parallel rulings about completing a sale. When someone sells a house, handing over the key completes it. When someone sells a flock, handing over the מַשְׁכּוּכִית completes it (רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ in the name of רַבִּי יַנַּאי). Both times the גמרא answers the same way: the real קנין is the normal one (חֲזָקָה or מְשִׁיכָה). The handed-over item only counts as the seller saying "go and acquire." The גמרא then asks what a מַשְׁכּוּכִית is: in בָּבֶל they say a bell, and רבי יעקב says the lead goat of the flock. Next, a new משנה lists rules about a בור: who is liable when a covered pit is found open, a proper cover versus an improper one, animals frightened by digging, vessels versus animals, and animals versus people. The גמרא asks how long the first person stays exempt, and רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן give three answers. It explains that a properly covered pit can still fail when the cover rots from inside. Finally, it asks about a cover strong enough for oxen but not camels, in a place where camels come only occasionally, and begins to bring a proof from the משנה that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Handing over the key completes the sale of a house
steps.stepSummary: This line ends a ruling that began just before this section: when someone sells a house, the buyer acquires it once the seller hands him the key.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once he handed him the key, the buyer has acquired the house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a ruling about selling a house: handing over the key completes the sale. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling sounds as if the key itself does the acquiring. That is surprising, because a key is not one of the normal ways of acquiring land. The next step will push on exactly this point.

phrases.english: once he handed him the key,
he has acquired it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the sale of a house, handing over the key completes the acquisition.

steps.title: What does the key add if there are already normal ways to acquire?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If the sale is done with money, money should be enough. If it is done with חֲזָקָה, the חֲזָקָה should be enough. Either way, the key seems to have no role.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he is buying with money, let him acquire with the money. If he is buying with חֲזָקָה, let him acquire with the חֲזָקָה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the key ruling. Land is already acquired through money or חֲזָקָה, so why would the key matter?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words look like a question, but they work as a challenge. Each normal method of acquiring land already works on its own. So the key seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? how do we picture it?
acquiring by doing an act of ownership on the property

phrases.english: What is the case?
If with money, let him acquire with the money!
If by taking possession, let him acquire by taking possession!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי בְּכַסְפָּא – לִיקְנֵי בְּכַסְפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the role of the key in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that handing over the key completes the sale.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each normal way of acquiring land works on its own, so the key has no job left to do.

steps.title: The key counts as permission to take possession
steps.stepSummary: The sale really happens through חֲזָקָה. Normally the seller must tell the buyer "go take possession and acquire." Handing over the key counts as saying exactly that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really the sale is by חֲזָקָה. For that, the seller has to tell the buyer "Go, take possession, and acquire." Handing him the key is the same as saying it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the key is not the קנין. It is the seller's permission for the buyer to do the חֲזָקָה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חֲזָקָה done when the seller is not there only works if the seller said "go take possession and acquire." The key acts as that statement. The actual acquiring is still done by the חֲזָקָה.

keyTerms.meaning: really, actually (the answer keeps one side of the question)
like someone who said to him

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the key itself acquires the house. The key only takes the place of the seller's words of permission. The חֲזָקָה is what actually acquires.

phrases.english: Actually, it is by taking possession,
and he needs to say to him:
"Go, take possession, and acquire";
and once he handed him the key,
it is like one who said to him:
"Go, take possession, and acquire."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the key's role: it is permission, not the act of acquiring.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The key seemed to be a separate, unnecessary way of acquiring.
steps.terutzMaskana: The קנין is חֲזָקָה. The key stands in for the words "go take possession and acquire."

steps.title: Handing over the lead animal completes the sale of a flock
steps.stepSummary: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ in the name of רַבִּי יַנַּאי: when someone sells a flock, the buyer acquires it once the seller hands him the מַשְׁכּוּכִית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ said in the name of רַבִּי יַנַּאי: if someone sells a flock to his friend, once he hands him the מַשְׁכּוּכִית, the buyer has acquired it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling that works just like the key ruling, this time about a flock of animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מַשְׁכּוּכִית is whatever the rest of the flock follows. Steps 8-9 give two views of what it is. Just as with the key, it sounds as if handing it over does the acquiring, and the next step questions that.

keyTerms.meaning: the lead animal that the flock follows

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יַנַּאי:
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said in the name of Rabbi Yannai:
One who sells a flock to his friend,
once he handed him the mashkukhit,
phrases.notes: The מַשְׁכּוּכִית is whatever the flock follows. Step 7 asks exactly what it is: a bell, or the lead goat.

phrases.english: he has acquired it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling to the key ruling, applied to animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the sale of a flock, handing over the lead animal completes the acquisition.

steps.title: What does the lead animal add if there are already normal ways to acquire?
steps.stepSummary: Same question as before. If the sale is by מְשִׁיכָה, the pulling should be enough. If it is by מְסִירָה, the handing over should be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If by pulling, let him acquire by pulling. If by handing over, let him acquire by handing over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same challenge it asked about the key, now about the lead animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals are acquired by מְשִׁיכָה (pulling) or מְסִירָה (handing over the reins or leash). Each of these works on its own. So why should handing over the lead animal matter?

keyTerms.meaning: acquiring by pulling the animal so it moves
acquiring by the seller handing over the animal's reins or leash

phrases.english: What is the case?
If by pulling, let him acquire by pulling!
If by handing over, let him acquire by handing over!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי בִּמְשִׁיכָה – לִיקְנֵי בִּמְשִׁיכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 4 the same way step 2 challenged step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that handing over the lead animal completes the sale.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מְשִׁיכָה and מְסִירָה each work without help, so the lead animal seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The lead animal counts as permission to pull
steps.stepSummary: The sale really happens through מְשִׁיכָה. Normally the seller must say "go pull and acquire." Handing over the lead animal counts as saying exactly that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really the sale is by מְשִׁיכָה. For that, the seller has to tell the buyer "Go, pull, and acquire." Handing him the lead animal is the same as saying it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers just as it did for the key. The lead animal is the seller's permission, and the מְשִׁיכָה is the real קנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling done when the seller is not there needs the seller's words "go pull and acquire." Handing over the lead animal counts as those words. The two rulings turn out to work the same way.
steps.whatToRemember: In both cases (the key to a house, the lead animal of a flock), the handed-over item is not the קנין. It counts as the seller saying "go and acquire," and the normal קנין (חֲזָקָה or מְשִׁיכָה) does the actual acquiring.

phrases.english: Actually, it is by pulling,
and he needs to say to him:
"Go, pull, and acquire,"
and once he handed him the mashkukhit,
it is like one who said to him:
"Go, pull, and acquire."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5 using the same reasoning as step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the lead animal's role: it is permission, not the act of acquiring.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lead animal seemed to be a separate, unnecessary way of acquiring.
steps.terutzMaskana: The קנין is מְשִׁיכָה. Handing over the lead animal stands in for the words "go pull and acquire."

steps.title: What is a מַשְׁכּוּכִית?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word מַשְׁכּוּכִית means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a מַשְׁכּוּכִית?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to define a hard word from רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ's statement. This sets up the two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 6 the גמרא explained that handing over the מַשְׁכּוּכִית counts as telling the buyer to pull and acquire. But we still don't know what the object actually is. Now the גמרא asks.

keyTerms.meaning: The thing the flock follows (it gets defined in the next steps)

phrases.english: What is a mashkukhit?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines a key word used in the statement just explained
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word מַשְׁכּוּכִית

steps.title: In בָּבֶל they say it is a bell
steps.stepSummary: Here in בָּבֶל they translate מַשְׁכּוּכִית as a bell.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here they translate it as a bell.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer is that the מַשְׁכּוּכִית is a bell. The flock follows its sound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this view, the seller hands over the bell, and the flock that follows the bell goes along with it. Handing it over is like saying "pull and acquire."

phrases.english: Here they translate it: a bell.
phrases.notes: "Here" means in בָּבֶל, where this גמרא was learned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מַשְׁכּוּכִית is a bell that the flock follows

steps.title: רבי יעקב says it is the lead goat
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב says the מַשְׁכּוּכִית is the goat that walks at the head of the flock.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב says: it is the goat that walks at the head of the flock.
steps.whatsHappening: A second answer is given. The מַשְׁכּוּכִית is not an object at all. It is the lead goat that the other animals follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two answers disagree about what is handed over: an object (a bell) or a living animal (the lead goat). Either way, the seller gives the buyer whatever the flock follows, so the ruling in step 6 works the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: At the head of the flock

phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov says:
the goat that goes at the head of the flock.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different definition from the bell
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מַשְׁכּוּכִית is the lead goat of the flock

steps.title: A Galilean's teaching about the leading goat
steps.stepSummary: A Galilean taught before רב חסדא that when a shepherd is angry at his flock, he makes the leading goat blind. This matches רבי יעקב's idea of a lead goat.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what a certain Galilean taught before רב חסדא: when the shepherd is angry at the flock, he makes the leader blind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי יעקב's explanation matches a known teaching. That teaching speaks of a goat that leads the flock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Galilean's lesson assumes the flock has a leading goat that everyone follows. If the leader is blind, the whole flock goes wrong. This backs up the idea that a flock really follows one lead goat.

keyTerms.meaning: The leader, the one who walks in front

steps.whatToRemember: The מַשְׁכּוּכִית is either a bell or the lead goat. Either way, it is the thing the flock follows, and handing it over counts as telling the buyer "pull and acquire."

phrases.english: As that certain Galilean taught
in front of Rav Chisda:
When the shepherd is angry at the flock,
he makes the leader blind.
phrases.notes: The message: when ה׳ is angry at the people, He gives them leaders who can't see where they're going.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדִדְרַשׁ הַהוּא גָּלִילָאָה עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יעקב's definition with a parallel teaching
steps.raayaObject: רבי יעקב's definition of מַשְׁכּוּכִית as the lead goat
steps.raayaSupportSource: The Galilean's teaching before רב חסדא about the shepherd blinding the leader

steps.title: The second person who leaves a pit uncovered is liable
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. The first person covered a pit. The second person found it uncovered and did not cover it, so the second person is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: The first one covered it. The second one came, found it uncovered, and did not cover it. The second one is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts with rules about a בור. Its first rule is that whoever last left the pit uncovered is responsible for damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first person did his job by covering the pit. Once the second person sees it open and leaves it that way, the responsibility moves to him.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
The first one covered it,
phrases.notes: "It" is a pit that two people were sharing or using, one after the other.

phrases.english: and the second came and found it uncovered,
and did not cover it: the second is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, unrelated to the sale discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the pit was found uncovered, the second person who left it uncovered is liable

steps.title: Covering properly exempts; covering improperly makes liable
steps.stepSummary: If the owner covered the pit properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt. If he did not cover it properly, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he covered it properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt. If he did not cover it properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a pair of rules. It all depends on whether the pit was covered the right way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A proper cover means the owner did what he had to do, so he does not pay. A cover that was not good enough counts as not doing his job, so he pays.

keyTerms.meaning: Properly, the way it should be

phrases.english: If he covered it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
If he did not cover it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with the rule about how well the pit was covered
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A proper cover exempts the owner; an improper cover makes him liable

steps.title: Falling forward or backward from the sound of digging
steps.stepSummary: If an animal fell forward because of the sound of digging, he is liable. If it fell backward because of the sound of digging, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it fell forward because of the sound of the digging, he is liable. If it fell backward because of the sound of the digging, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה deals with an animal that got scared by the noise of someone digging and fell. Which way it fell decides the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Falling forward makes the digger liable. Falling backward exempts him. The משנה states the rule without explaining it here.

phrases.english: If it fell forward from the sound of the digging, he is liable;
phrases.notes: The picture is someone digging a pit, and a passing animal gets frightened by the noise.

phrases.english: backward from the sound of the digging, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new case to the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal that falls forward from the digging noise makes the digger liable; one that falls backward does not

steps.title: Liable for the animal, exempt for its vessels
steps.stepSummary: If an ox and its vessels fell in and the vessels broke, or a donkey and its gear fell in and the gear tore, the pit owner pays for the animal but not for the vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: If an ox and its vessels fell into it and they broke, or a donkey and its gear fell in and it tore, he is liable for the animal and exempt for the vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a rule that splits one accident into two parts. The pit owner pays for the animal but not for the things it was carrying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though everything fell into the same pit, the law treats the animal and the objects differently. A בור makes its owner pay for animals, but not for כלים.

keyTerms.meaning: Its vessels or gear (what the animal was carrying or wearing)

steps.whatToRemember: Under the law of בור, the owner pays for an animal that falls in, but not for the כלים it was carrying.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the owner pays for everything because it all fell together. The משנה clearly splits it: the animal is paid for, but the vessels are not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule shows that the damage law of בור only covers certain kinds of losses, not every loss that happens in a pit.

phrases.english: If an ox and its vessels fell into it, and they broke,
or a donkey and its gear, and they tore,
he is liable for the animal,
and exempt for the vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the final case of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The pit owner is liable for the animal but exempt for the vessels

steps.title: Impaired animals bring liability, but people do not
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends: if a deaf, mentally impaired or very young ox falls into the pit, the owner is liable. If a boy, girl, slave or maidservant falls in, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a deaf, foolish or young ox fell into the pit, the owner must pay. If a boy or a girl, a slave or a maidservant fell in, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list of pit cases. It tells us which kinds of victims make the pit owner pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that is deaf, confused or very young is easier to trap, but the owner still pays for it. People who fall in, however, do not make him liable here. The line is drawn between animals and people, not between smart and impaired victims.

keyTerms.meaning: Mentally impaired, foolish (here describing the ox)
Young, small (here a very young ox)

steps.confusionAlert: Usually חרש, שוטה וקטן means three kinds of people. Here all three words describe the ox. The people in this משנה are the בן, בת, עבד and אמה, and for them he is exempt.

phrases.english: If an ox fell into it
that was deaf, foolish, or young, he is liable.
phrases.notes: All three words describe the ox, not people.

phrases.english: If a boy or a girl,
a slave or a maidservant fell in, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of pit cases from step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liable for impaired or young animals; exempt for human victims.

steps.title: How long is the first person exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking how long the first person, who covered the pit, stays exempt once it becomes uncovered.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: And the first person, until when is he exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and goes back to the משנה's first case (step 11). It asks how long the first person stays free of blame. This question sets up the three opinions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the first person covered the pit and the second person is liable. But the first person still owns the pit. At some point, if he does nothing, the responsibility should come back to him. The גמרא wants to know exactly when that happens.

keyTerms.meaning: The first person (the one who covered the pit)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
And the first, until when is he exempt?
phrases.notes: This is the person from step 11 who covered the pit before it was found uncovered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the first case of the משנה (step 11) to ask about its time limit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much time passes before the first person becomes responsible again for an uncovered pit.

steps.title: Three opinions on how much time the first person has
steps.stepSummary: רב says he is exempt only until he could know. שמואל says until people could tell him. רבי יוחנן says until people tell him and he can hire workers, cut cedars and cover it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: as long as it takes for him to know. שמואל said: as long as it takes for people to tell him. רבי יוחנן said: as long as it takes for people to tell him, for him to hire workers, cut cedar trees and cover it.
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים answer the question, and each gives the first person a longer amount of time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב gives the shortest time: once he could have known, he is responsible. שמואל adds the time it takes for others to notice and tell him. רבי יוחנן adds even more time, enough to actually fix the pit, because knowing alone does not cover it.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: time to know. שמואל: time to be told. רבי יוחנן: time to be told AND to fix it.

phrases.english: Rav said: for as long as it takes him to know.
And Shmuel said: for as long as it takes for them to inform him.
And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
for as long as it takes for them to inform him, and for him to hire workers,
and cut cedars, and cover it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16 with three opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The exemption lasts until he could know (רב), until he could be told (שמואל), or until he could be told and fix the pit (רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: How could an animal fall into a properly covered pit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that he is exempt if the pit was properly covered, then asks how an animal could fall in if the cover was proper.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he covered it properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt. But if he covered it properly, how did it fall in?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line of the משנה from step 12 again. It does this to ask how that case could actually happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A proper cover should hold the animal. If the animal still fell in, it seems the cover was not proper after all. So the גמרא needs a realistic picture of this case.

phrases.english: If he covered it properly,
and an ox or a donkey fell into it,
and died, he is exempt.
Since he covered it properly, how did it fall?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the time-limit question to the next line of the משנה (step 12).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A realistic way an animal could fall into a properly covered pit.

steps.title: The cover rotted from inside
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בר בר חנה explains that the cover rotted from within, so the damage could not be seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק בר בר חנה said: it is a case where the cover became worm-eaten from inside.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא answers the question by describing the case. The cover was fine when he put it on, but it rotted from the inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rot was hidden inside the cover, so the owner had no way of knowing it was weak. That is why the cover still counts as proper and he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר בַּר חָנָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar bar Ḥana said:
It is where it rotted from inside it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר בַּר חָנָה: שֶׁהִתְלִיעַ מִתּוֹכוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The cover rotted from inside without the owner knowing.

steps.title: A cover strong enough for oxen but not for camels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about a cover that holds oxen but not camels. Camels came and weakened it, then oxen came and fell in. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: if he covered it with a cover that can hold oxen but cannot hold camels, and camels came and weakened it, and then oxen came and fell in, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question about a cover that was strong enough for one kind of animal but not for another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the oxen that fell, the cover was good enough. But it broke only because heavier camels had weakened it first. So the question is whether this counts as a proper cover or a careless one.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised to them

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
If he covered it with a cover that is able
to hold up under oxen,
but cannot hold up under camels;
and camels came and weakened it,
and then oxen came and fell into it, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the idea of a proper cover from steps 18-19 and asks about a cover that is proper only for some animals.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a cover strong enough for oxen counts as proper when camels weakened it and oxen then fell in.

steps.title: Either he was careless or it was beyond his control
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the question: if camels are common there, he was careless; if not, it was beyond his control. Either way the answer seems clear.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: what is the case? If camels are common there, he is careless! And if camels are not common there, it was beyond his control!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the question itself, saying there seems to be nothing to ask. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא will need to find a case that really is in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If camels often pass by, he should have built a cover strong enough for them, so he was careless. If camels never come, he could not have planned for them, so he is not to blame. Since both possibilities have a clear answer, the question seems to have no real doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?
Forced by things beyond his control

phrases.english: They said: What are the circumstances?
If camels are commonly found, he is negligent!

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי דְּלָא שְׁכִיחִי גְּמַלִּים – אָנוּס הוּא!
phrases.english: And if camels are not commonly found, he is a victim of circumstances beyond his control!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the question of step 20 by showing both possible cases already have a clear answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question about the camels and the oxen in step 20.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Splitting the case into common camels (careless) and uncommon camels (beyond his control) leaves no real doubt to ask about.

steps.title: The case is where camels come only sometimes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the question is about a place where camels come occasionally. It then restates the question: is the pit owner a פושע for not expecting them, or an אנוס since none were there at the time?
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed where camels come only occasionally. Do we say that since they come sometimes, he is negligent, because he should have had it in mind? Or perhaps, since right now there are none around, he is a victim of circumstances?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 21 by pointing to a middle case: camels come, but only once in a while. This turns the question back into a real, open question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 said the question was obvious: if camels are common he is a פושע, and if they never come he is an אנוס. The answer is that there is an in-between case where both sides make sense. Either he should have expected the camels, or he is excused because at the moment none were around.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for... (the case is limited to a specific situation)
To bring it to mind, to anticipate it
A victim of circumstances beyond one's control (and so exempt)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the animals. The camels only weakened the cover. The oxen are the ones that fell in. The question is whether the owner should have planned for the camels.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where they come occasionally;
phrases.notes: "They" means the camels from the question in step 20.

phrases.english: do we say: since they come occasionally,

phrases.aramaic: פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא, דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ אַסּוֹקֵי אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ;
phrases.english: he is negligent, for he should have kept it in mind;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דְּהַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת לֵיכָּא –
phrases.english: or perhaps, since right now at any rate there are none,
he is a victim of circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the push-back of step 21 by narrowing the case to one where camels come only occasionally.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question seemed pointless, since either camels are common (פושע) or not (אנוס).
steps.terutzMaskana: There is a real in-between case of occasional camels, where both sides are reasonable, so the question stands.

steps.title: Bringing the משנה about a properly covered pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer the question from the משנה: if he covered the pit properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he covered it properly, and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה as a possible proof for the camel question. This step only quotes the source. The analysis comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a proper cover makes the owner exempt. The גמרא will try to show that 'proper' here means proper only for oxen, which would match our camel case. If so, the משנה would be ruling אנוס.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
if he covered it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the question from step 22 using the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The camel question: is the owner exempt (אנוס) when occasional camels weakened the cover?
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: כסהו כראוי ונפל לתוכו שור או חמור ומת פטור

steps.title: Working out what kind of proper cover the משנה means
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה describes. If the cover was strong enough even for camels, how did the animal fall? So it must mean a cover proper only for oxen.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it was proper for oxen and proper for camels, how did they fall in? Rather, is it not that it was proper for oxen,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is building its proof by ruling out one reading of the משנה. It pushes toward the reading that the cover was strong only enough for oxen. The sentence continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cover strong enough even for camels could not be weakened by camels, so the fall would make no sense. That leaves a cover proper for oxen but not for camels, which matches our question. The גמרא is setting up the conclusion that the משנה rules him exempt in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What case is this?
If you say (introduces a reading about to be rejected)
Rather, is it not that... (introduces the reading the proof needs)

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say it was proper for oxen and proper for camels,
how did they fall in?
Rather, is it not that it was proper for oxen,

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְכָרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the משנה just quoted to show it is talking about our camel case.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the owner is exempt when the cover was fit for oxen but not camels
steps.raayaSupportSource: Process of elimination on the משנה's word כראוי: a camel-proof cover could not be breached, so it must mean oxen-proof only.
